params.question: In the case scenario, the tribal woman's anaemia and hypertension went undetected until 28 weeks. Which programme failure was most directly responsible for this delayed detection?

answers.text: JSSK, because it failed to provide free iron and folic acid tablets

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: JSSK does entitle her to free IFA tablets, but the core failure was in detection, not treatment. She never entered the system at all — no one was monitoring her pregnancy to catch these complications.

answers.text: RMNCH+A tracking, because her pregnancy should have been monitored through ASHA home visits and a Mother–Child Protection card from the first trimester

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Under RMNCH+A, every pregnancy should be tracked on a Mother–Child Protection card, and the ASHA worker is expected to make four home visits. That tracking would have caught her anaemia and hypertension well before 28 weeks.

answers.text: RBSK, because mobile health teams should have screened her during their visits

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: RBSK screens children aged 0–18 years for the 4Ds (birth defects, diseases, deficiencies, and developmental delays). It does not cover pregnant women.

answers.text: Mission Indradhanush, because she missed her scheduled immunisations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mission Indradhanush is an intensive immunisation catch-up campaign for children under 2 and pregnant women who missed vaccines. It does not address antenatal detection of anaemia or hypertension.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the case: the woman was never tracked. Under RMNCH+A, her ASHA worker should have made four home visits and documented her pregnancy on a Mother–Child Protection card. That tracking would have detected the anaemia and hypertension much earlier.
Well done. The RMNCH+A tracking system — ASHA home visits and the MCP card — is designed to catch exactly these complications early. When that system fails, women reach care dangerously late.

params.question: The RMNCH+A framework insists that all five strategic areas must advance together rather than in isolation. Which of the following best explains why?

answers.text: Because the central government allocates funding equally across all five areas and none can be left unspent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The rationale is clinical, not financial. The narration explains that each stage feeds the next biologically — for instance, unaddressed maternal anaemia drives low birth weight and newborn mortality, regardless of how much is spent on immunisation.

answers.text: Because each of the five areas is delivered by a separate dedicated workforce that depends on the others

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration states the opposite: all five areas are delivered by the same community health workers. The reason for moving together is the life-course continuum, not workforce dependency.

answers.text: Because each stage of the life-course continuum feeds the next, and a gap at any stage undermines the gains made at others

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A healthy adolescent is more likely to have a healthy pregnancy; a well-managed delivery reduces newborn sepsis risk; and proper newborn care improves childhood survival. Breaking this chain at any point leads to preventable deaths.

answers.text: Because international agencies require simultaneous progress in all five areas before releasing development aid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The justification is epidemiological, not related to international funding conditions. Gains in one area (e.g., skilled birth attendance) are eroded if the preceding or succeeding stage (e.g., postnatal care) is neglected.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the narration's key example: good immunisation coverage means little if maternal anaemia goes unaddressed, because anaemia drives low birth weight and newborn mortality. Each stage of the life-course feeds the next — that is why all five must advance together.

Exactly. The continuum-of-care principle is central to RMNCH+A — interventions across adolescence, pregnancy, delivery, the newborn period, and childhood are biologically linked, so all must progress in step.

interactions.label: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Mission Indradhanush from ICDS?

params.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Mission Indradhanush from ICDS?

answers.text: Mission Indradhanush provides supplementary nutrition, while ICDS focuses on immunisation catch-up

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the two programmes. Supplementary nutrition is one of the six services delivered by ICDS through Anganwadi centres. Mission Indradhanush is the immunisation campaign.

answers.text: Both programmes were launched together in 2014 as part of a single NHM initiative

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ICDS was launched in 1975 — nearly four decades before Mission Indradhanush (2014). They serve very different functions within the child health framework.

answers.text: Mission Indradhanush operates through Anganwadi centres, while ICDS uses mobile health teams

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is reversed. ICDS operates through Anganwadi centres with the Anganwadi Worker running day-to-day services. Mission Indradhanush uses health workers who actively track down missed children in high-focus districts.

answers.text: Mission Indradhanush is a targeted immunisation catch-up campaign launched in 2014, while ICDS is a comprehensive early childhood programme delivering six services through Anganwadi centres since 1975

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Mission Indradhanush responds to stalled immunisation coverage by actively finding unimmunised children in high-focus districts. ICDS has run since 1975 as India's largest early childhood programme, providing nutrition, immunisation, health check-ups, referrals, preschool education, and health education.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: Mission Indradhanush (2014) is a targeted immunisation catch-up for high-focus districts where coverage had stalled at around 44–65%. ICDS (1975) is India's largest early childhood programme, delivering six services — nutrition, immunisation, health check-ups, referrals, preschool education, and health education — through village Anganwadi centres.

Well done. Mission Indradhanush is an intensive catch-up campaign for stalled immunisation, while ICDS is a long-standing comprehensive early childhood platform. Knowing this contrast helps you understand which programme addresses which gap.

params.question: The narration cautions that India's improved national health averages can be misleading. Which of the following best explains why this matters for clinicians?

answers.text: Because the data collection methods used by NHM surveys are statistically unreliable

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration does not question the reliability of the data. It points out that real disparities between states and populations are hidden by aggregate figures.

answers.text: Because national averages conceal stark inter-state disparities and under-covered populations, and clinicians will encounter these local failures directly in practice

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. States like Kerala and Tamil Nadu are far ahead of Bihar, UP, and Rajasthan. Tribal communities, nomadic populations, and urban slum dwellers remain under-covered. As a doctor, your patients are individuals from specific communities — not national averages.

answers.text: Because all the improvement has occurred in urban areas, while rural health outcomes have actually worsened

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration does not say rural outcomes have worsened. Institutional delivery gains have been substantial in rural areas. The disparity is between high-performing and low-performing states, and between reached and unreached populations.

answers.text: Because private healthcare is excluded from NHM statistics, making government programme data appear artificially favourable

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The narration does not raise this concern. The key analytical point is that national averages hide the experience of specific states and populations where outcomes remain poor despite overall progress.

overallFeedback.feedback: The narration makes a specific analytical point: national averages hide local failures. About 24% of children are incompletely immunised, anaemia has worsened (67% of children, 57% of women), and states like Bihar and UP still lag far behind Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Clinicians encounter individuals from these communities, not averages.

Exactly. Impressive national averages mask the reality that 24% of children remain incompletely immunised, anaemia has actually worsened, and inter-state disparities persist. As a clinician, you will see these gaps first-hand.
